newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major pins re-election hopes on economy.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major pins re-election hopes on economy.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major pinned his re-election hopes on fresh official figures on Wednesday showing the British economy was in good shape as a new rift opened in his ruling Conservative Party over Europe.
Latest polls showed the opposition Labour Party's lead widening in the run-up to the May 1 general election.

The Conservatives, seeking a fifth consecutive term, were rocked late on Tuesday when two junior ministers flouted government policy by declaring their opposition to Britain joining a single European currency.
Junior health minister John Horam's announcement in his election manifesto contradicted Major's "wait and see" policy and led to calls from opposition parties for his sacking.

"I personally am opposed to a single currency but I think the right line is to stay at the negotiating table..and wait and see what happens," Horam said in a television interview, denying that he was out of line with government policy.
James Paice, a junior education minister, was also at odds with the government in his manifesto, saying a single currency would lead to European political union.
Mayor's party suffered a further blow when the Times newspaper said another nine ministers, including two in cabinet posts, were breaching the government line in private.

The Conservatives, trailing by up to 21 points in the latest opinions polls, had hoped the tide was turning for them and that good news would be on the way in the shape of a string of economic figures due out on Wednesday.

The jobless figures were expected to show 45,000 more people were taken out of the dole queues in March. British unemployment has fallen to a six-year low, having dropped consistently over the last 30 months.
But British newspapers poured cold water on the figures, saying the government had admitted understating jobless data in an application for funds submitted to the European Commission.
The Daily Mirror, which had leaked the figures for the past two months, said the official jobless total was expected to be 1,700,000 but in reality it was much higher.
"Experts say the real figure is 4-5 million," the Mirror said.
Earlier on Tuesday, Major told a packed audience of 2,000 people in London that the economy was in good shape and he would keep it that way.
It would allow him to improve education and health services and to help more "have-nots", while always jealously guarding Britain's interests in Europe, he said.

His message has yet to slice away at Labour's lead. An opinion poll in Wednesday's Guardian newspaper put Labour 14 points ahead, up two from last week. Another in the Daily Telegraph put the lead at a staggering 21 points, up three from last week.

"Nobody should go into the general election thinking that because the economy is benign now that it cannot be thrown away by the wrong policies on spending, on tax, the wrong policies on Europe, the wrong policies on regulation and trade union reform," Major told his audience.
